rv.q: Gough is flinty and fierce and utterly compelling as she descends into derangement.
Her unravelling is painful to watch, and her performance really does rise to the heights of Greek drama, intense and unstoppably tragic.
Every move she makes is precise, vital, mesmerising.
This histrionic, hyper-stylised version from director Ebenezer Bamgboye may be aiming to recapture some of that original confrontational force, but overshoots the mark.
The musical, physical and theatrical artistry is so vibrantly clear in this performance that the story almost fades into an experimental backdrop for exploring the violence of desire.
This revival lives and breathes through the temperature of its performances, with Gough’s Abbie and Momoh’s Eben ensuring the farm’s suffocating heat feels palpable.
But while you can’t help admire his heated, guttural vision, it stretches out the play’s action and ultimately threatens to overwhelm the drama it seeks to illuminate.

He throws everything at an expressionistic, visceral production that is always gripping – but all its inventiveness and commitment can’t quite raise the play to the level of insight that truly great O’Neill can achieve.
Desire Under the Elms is well acted with stunning lighting and focused direction.
Indeed the 2 hour and 40 minutes running time (including interval) vastly outstays its welcome.
This Desire Under The Elms is a stunning composition, driven by unbridled talent and passion.
Bamgboye’s production features a bewildering mix of bronze lighting, intrusive music, shouting and random dance sequences which obscure any meaning or message behind the classic.
Though it is admirable in its attempts to bring something new to a Eugene O’Neill classic, the result is a confused and underbaked production that wasn’t quite what I desired.
It’s hard to imagine American theatre before this indelibly powerful if flawed work. And that it was the greatest American tragedy, indeed play ever written when it opened in 1924.
It has an interesting story at its heart with the potential to shock and move, but it's bogged down with excess dialogue and can't punch through.
I could appreciate the intensity of what was unfolding without always feeling emotionally connected to it.

cn.t: Mixed reception for Bamgboye's hyper-stylised O'Neill revival: Kelly Gough earns near-universal praise, but critics are divided on whether the bold, maximalist direction dazzles or overwhelms.
